name: X-linked Reticulate Pigmentary Disorder
aliases: X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder with systemic manifestations

clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive multisystem disorder caused by a recurrent deep-intronic variant in POLA1, the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase alpha, that reduces POLA1 expression.
Loss of POLA1-dependent cytosolic nucleic-acid synthesis leads to unopposed type I interferon activation, placing the disorder among the type I interferonopathies.
Affected males show generalised reticulate grey-brown hyperpigmentation developing in infancy, with a distinctive facies of frontally upswept hair and flaring, arched eyebrows.

Recurrent respiratory infections progressing to bronchiectasis, intractable infantile diarrhoea or enterocolitis with failure to thrive, and inflammatory keratitis with corneal scarring and photophobia are cardinal systemic features.
Hypohidrosis, recurrent urinary tract problems such as urethral stricture and stones, and episodes of sterile inflammation are common.
Carrier females are typically asymptomatic apart from linear hyperpigmentation following the lines of Blaschko, reflecting X-inactivation.
Despite the recurrent infections, the immune phenotype is one of dysregulation and autoinflammation rather than a classic immunodeficiency.
Systemic involvement distinguishes it from purely cutaneous reticulate disorders such as acropigmentation of Kitamura and Dowling-Degos disease.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder is caused by a recurrent deep-intronic single-nucleotide variant in POLA1, the gene encoding the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase alpha. The variant induces aberrant splicing that reduces POLA1 protein levels. Beyond its canonical role in initiating nuclear DNA replication, DNA polymerase alpha synthesises cytosolic RNA:DNA species that normally restrain the type I interferon response; when POLA1 is deficient this brake is lost and there is chronic, unopposed production of type I interferon, so the disorder behaves as a type I interferonopathy with autoinflammatory tissue damage. The reticulate pigmentation, recurrent sterile and infective inflammation of the lungs, gut, cornea, and urinary tract, and the characteristic dysmorphism all stem from this interferon-driven dysregulation combined with partial replication stress. Because POLA1 is X-linked, hemizygous males are affected while heterozygous females show only Blaschko-linear hyperpigmentation corresponding to the pattern of lyonisation.
additionalDifferentials: Incontinentia pigmenti (IKBKG/NEMO) with Blaschko-linear pigmentation but preceding vesicular and verrucous stages and a different systemic profile.
Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura (ADAM10) and Dowling-Degos disease, which are cutaneous only without systemic disease.
Dyskeratosis congenita with reticulate pigmentation, nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia, and bone-marrow failure.
Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome (KRT14) with reticulate pigmentation, hypohidrosis, and absent dermatoglyphics.
Other type I interferonopathies such as Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome and STING-associated vasculopathy with overlapping inflammatory features.
Chronic granulomatous disease and other primary immunodeficiencies presenting with recurrent infections and colitis.
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular testing for the recurrent intronic POLA1 variant, which standard exome pipelines may miss.
Interferon signature or gene-expression testing supporting a type I interferonopathy.
Skin biopsy of reticulate lesions and examination of the mother for Blaschko-linear pigmentation.
Ophthalmological assessment with slit-lamp examination for keratitis and corneal scarring.
High-resolution chest imaging and respiratory review for recurrent infection and bronchiectasis.
Gastrointestinal evaluation with endoscopy and histology for enterocolitis and failure to thrive.
Immunological work-up with cultures during infective episodes, and urological imaging for stricture or stones.
redFlags: Sight-threatening keratitis with corneal scarring requiring urgent ophthalmology input.
Recurrent pneumonia progressing to bronchiectasis or respiratory failure.
Intractable infantile diarrhoea with failure to thrive and dehydration.
Systemic inflammatory flares or sepsis in an infant with reticulate pigmentation and the characteristic facies.
Urinary obstruction from stricture or stones threatening renal function.
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable and depends on the severity of recurrent respiratory, gastrointestinal, and ocular disease; some affected males have significant morbidity and early mortality from infection or its complications, while others survive into adulthood. Carrier females generally have a normal lifespan with only cutaneous findings.
pitfalls: The causative POLA1 variant is deep-intronic and can be missed by standard exome sequencing, delaying diagnosis.
Misreading recurrent infections as a primary immunodeficiency and overlooking the underlying interferonopathy.
Dismissing a mother's Blaschko-linear pigmentation, which is a key clue to X-linked inheritance.
Attributing the multisystem disease to the pigmentation alone, or confusing it with purely cutaneous reticulate disorders.
Overlooking treatable ocular and pulmonary complications while focusing on the skin.
references: Inborn Errors of Immunity reference texts
management: Prompt antimicrobial treatment of recurrent respiratory, urinary and gastrointestinal infections
Airway clearance and chest physiotherapy with respiratory surveillance for evolving bronchiectasis
Nutritional support and gastroenterology management of enterocolitis and failure to thrive
Ophthalmic care with ocular lubrication and specialist treatment of inflammatory keratitis and corneal scarring
Consideration of interferon-pathway-directed therapy such as JAK inhibition, reflecting the disorder's nature as a type I interferonopathy
Urological management of recurrent urinary problems including urethral stricture and stones
Multidisciplinary follow-up across respiratory, gastroenterology, ophthalmology and immunology
Genetic counselling with targeted testing for the deep-intronic POLA1 variant and carrier assessment of mothers
